plot: Odo and Mothwick follow the true story of Blood Falls, Antarctica: in 1911 geologist Griffith Taylor of Scott's Terra Nova expedition finds Taylor Glacier pouring blood-red water and blames red algae; a century later scientists find salty, oxygen-free water sealed under the ice for up to two million years with microbes that breathe iron, and 2017 radar traces the brine to the falls; the twist is that it was never blood or algae but iron rusting the instant the clear brine meets the air — the clue Mothwick spotted at the start.

beats.say: 1911, Antarctica: explorers found a glacier pouring red onto white ice.
Red? Like blood? Why would a glacier bleed?
A true story. The place is still called Blood Falls.
Write it down. Red ice, right at the end of the glacier.
Griffith Taylor was a geologist on Captain Scott's Terra Nova expedition.
The glacier would soon carry his name. Taylor Glacier.
Look closer, Odo. Where it first comes out, it isn't red yet.
So it turns red... out here, in the open air?
This is the McMurdo Dry Valleys. Almost no snow falls here.
No trees. No grass. Nothing grows. And yet the ice runs red.
Taylor's team had one idea: red algae, tiny living plants.
Algae. It must be algae, staining the ice.
But how does anything grow inside a frozen glacier?
For almost a hundred years, algae stayed the answer in the books.
If it isn't algae, Odo, then this glacier is hiding something.
Much later, scientists came back and collected the red water.
It's salty. Far saltier than melted glacier ice should be.
And it had almost no oxygen in it at all.
There's life in it. Microbes. Living in total darkness.
Sealed under the ice for up to two million years.
Two million years... and they never once saw the sun?
New true story every day. Subscribe so you never miss one.
No light. No air. So how do they stay alive down there?
They breathe iron. Iron washed out of the rock under the glacier.
Their pool is thought to lie under four hundred meters of ice.
But how does salty water reach the falls from so deep?
In 2017, a team used radar to look inside Taylor Glacier.
One antenna sends, one listens. Salty water shows up bright.
They found brine flowing under the ice, toward the falls.
Liquid water, in the coldest glacier known to have flowing water.
Salt makes it harder to freeze. And freezing water gives off heat.
That explains the water, Odo. Not the blood.
Here is the answer. It was never blood. And never algae.
The brine carries iron. Under the ice, in the dark, it's clear.
The moment it touches the air, the iron rusts. Bright red.
That's why it wasn't red when it first came out!
A glacier bleeding rust, from a lake sealed for two million years.
The red water runs down into Lake Bonney, frozen below.
Taylor saw the color in 1911. The reason took about a century.
Now those microbes help scientists think about life on other worlds.
Icy moons. Frozen planets. If life hides here, it could hide there.
So Blood Falls isn't a wound. It's a doorway.
Still alive in the dark. Still painting the ice red.
Liked this? The Gloucester sea serpent story is next on the channel.
Have you heard a story like this one? Tell me in the comments.
